headline: Go-Ai gateway simplifies LLM provider setup for developers
summary: A new Go-based HTTP gateway centralizes provider credentials and model management, freeing applications to focus on core features.
details: Developers often face repetitive setup tasks when integrating with various LLM providers, including managing API keys, comparing streaming responses, and ensuring provider compatibility. This can distract from the core goal of testing and developing new features.

To address this, a new project called Go-Ai has been developed. It acts as a small, dedicated HTTP gateway that provides a stable interface for application backends to interact with LLM providers, handling the complexities of provider-specific details.

Go-Ai is built with Go, chosen for its pragmatic approach to building compact services with clear failure cases. The gateway's design deliberately avoids becoming a full-fledged AI platform or agent runtime, focusing solely on simplifying the provider integration layer.

The gateway allows applications to use local aliases for models instead of provider-specific slugs. This means changes to upstream model names or provider availability can be managed within Go-Ai without needing to update multiple application codebases.
This approach centralizes provider credentials and configuration in one place, ensuring that each new application doesn't have to rediscover and re-implement these setup procedures independently.

While projects like LiteLLM, LangChain, and Vercel AI SDK offer broader functionalities, Go-Ai is designed for developers who need a simpler, more focused solution that can be deployed alongside their applications.

The gateway supports OpenAI-compatible chat requests and can proxy SSE streams. It also handles separate proxy routes for speech-to-text and text-to-speech, keeping voice functionality distinct from core chat operations.

Crucially, Go-Ai does not execute tools itself. It passes tool-related payloads through, leaving the application to manage user permissions, access controls, and acceptable side effects, maintaining a clear separation of concerns.

headline_marked: [[AI graveyard]]: 42% of AI initiatives are abandoned, startups shut down
headline: AI graveyard: 42% of AI initiatives are abandoned, startups shut down
summary: From Relay to Notion Mail, AI startups are struggling as big tech integrates similar features. Even giants like OpenAI and Apple face AI project casualties.
details: Relay, an AI workflow automation tool, has shut down entirely, becoming another casualty in the growing "AI graveyard." The startup struggled as larger platforms like OpenAI and Google integrated similar AI automation features into their own products.

The trend extends beyond startups; S&P Global Market Intelligence reports that approximately 42% of AI initiatives are abandoned by their parent companies due to challenges like funding, technical hurdles, competition, or weak user demand.

Even tech giants are not immune. OpenAI's attempt to transform ChatGPT into a "super app" with integrated "Chat," "Codex," and "Work" modes faced user backlash and was quickly rolled back. The company has also discontinued standalone apps like ChatGPT Atlas and Operator, folding their features into ChatGPT.

Apple's AI-powered Siri also faced delays and engineering issues, contributing to a $250 million settlement over marketing claims. The improved Siri is now rolling out in beta, but its development path highlights the complexities of AI integration.

Microsoft's Recall feature, pitched as a "photographic memory" for Windows PCs, was delayed for nearly a year due to significant privacy and security concerns. Despite redesigns, a recent demonstration showed a tool capable of extracting captured data, reigniting doubts about its security.
Notion Mail, an AI-focused email product, is scheduled to shut down on September 22nd, as users opted for separate AI agents to manage their inboxes instead of the integrated solution.

Relay, an AI workflow automation tool, has shut down entirely, becoming another casualty in the growing "AI graveyard." The startup struggled as larger platforms like OpenAI and Google integrated similar AI automation features into their own products.

The trend extends beyond startups; S&P Global Market Intelligence reports that approximately 42% of AI initiatives are abandoned by their parent companies due to challenges like funding, technical hurdles, competition, or weak user demand.

Even tech giants are not immune. OpenAI's attempt to transform ChatGPT into a "super app" with integrated "Chat," "Codex," and "Work" modes faced user backlash and was quickly rolled back. The company has also discontinued standalone apps like ChatGPT Atlas and Operator, folding their features into ChatGPT.

Apple's AI-powered Siri also faced delays and engineering issues, contributing to a $250 million settlement over marketing claims. The improved Siri is now rolling out in beta, but its development path highlights the complexities of AI integration.

Microsoft's Recall feature, pitched as a "photographic memory" for Windows PCs, was delayed for nearly a year due to significant privacy and security concerns. Despite redesigns, a recent demonstration showed a tool capable of extracting captured data, reigniting doubts about its security.

Notion Mail, an AI-focused email product, is scheduled to shut down on September 22nd, as users opted for separate AI agents to manage their inboxes instead of the integrated solution.
